strategies.name: Big picture first
strategies.summary: See the whole before the details.
strategies.use_when: details are drowning the person, or they cannot see why the parts matter.
steps: Stop the details. Ask: "What is this whole thing for, in one sentence?"
Draw the whole thing as 3 to 5 big blocks. No details yet.
Ask which block matters most right now.
Zoom into that one block only. Leave the others closed.
strategies.shared_by: starter strategy, written for v0.1.0. Waiting for community stories.
strategies.inspired_by: dyslexic leaders described by Fortune as focusing on the big picture

strategies.name: Build a model
strategies.summary: Make the idea with your hands, then move the pieces.
strategies.use_when: an idea has parts that fit together, and words keep them flat.
steps: Ask what the parts are. Give each one a physical stand-in: a sticky note, a coin, a box on screen.
Lay them out so their position means something: near, far, above, inside.
Move one piece and ask what changes.
When the layout feels right, put it back into words.
strategies.inspired_by: Material reasoning in The Dyslexic Advantage by Brock and Fernette Eide, and the clay models of the Davis method

strategies.name: Build a team around your gaps
strategies.summary: Do what you're great at. Hand the rest to someone who's great at it.
strategies.use_when: the person is doing everything alone, including the parts that drain them.
steps: List the tasks of the project. Mark each one: energises me, or drains me.
For each draining task, ask who could do it well: a colleague, a friend, a tool, Claude.
Keep the tasks only you can do. Hand off one draining task this week.
Agree how you will check the result, so handing off feels safe.
strategies.inspired_by: Richard Branson on delegating what he found difficult, and Kinko's founder Paul Orfalea

strategies.name: Draw it as a map
strategies.summary: Put the problem in the middle, and find the knot.
strategies.use_when: the person is stuck and the problem is going round in their head.
steps: Put the problem in the middle, in a few words.
Ask what connects to it. Draw each answer as a branch.
Draw lines between branches that affect each other.
Ask: "Looking at the map, where is the knot?" Work on that part first.

strategies.name: Explain it with a movie
strategies.summary: Explain a situation through a movie scene everyone can picture.
strategies.use_when: a situation is hard to explain in plain words, or people are not getting it.
steps: Find the heart of the situation in one line: who wants what, and what is in the way.
Pick a movie scene or a well-known image with the same shape. Ask the person if they know it.
Explain the situation through the scene: who is who, and what happens next.
Come back to the real situation, and say what the scene teaches.

strategies.name: Find another path
strategies.summary: When the usual way is blocked, find three others.
strategies.use_when: the normal way is blocked, too slow, or does not fit the person.
steps: Name the usual way in one line, and what blocks it.
List three other paths. Make at least one of them unusual.
For each path, say what it costs in one line.
Let the person choose. Then plan only the chosen path.
strategies.shared_by: Miguel Vicente, and a starter strategy for v0.1.0.

strategies.name: Go and look
strategies.summary: Skip the report. Go where it happens and watch.
strategies.use_when: the person is trying to understand a problem through documents, and it is not working.
steps: Ask where the problem actually happens: a shop, a screen, a phone call, a factory.
Plan a short visit or a short call. 30 minutes is enough.
Write 3 questions to ask, and 3 things to watch.
Afterwards, Claude turns what they saw into a map.
strategies.inspired_by: Kinko's founder Paul Orfalea, who learned his business by walking the stores and talking to people

strategies.name: Jump to the answer, then check
strategies.summary: Trust the leap to the answer, then prove it step by step.
strategies.use_when: the person already feels the answer, but cannot yet explain the steps.
steps: Ask for the answer first: "What does your gut say?"
Write it down as a claim.
Work backwards together: what would have to be true for it to be right?
Check those things. Keep the answer, change it, or drop it.
strategies.inspired_by: Charles Schwab, who says he gets to the conclusion much faster than others

strategies.name: Keep the message simple
strategies.summary: If it takes a page to explain, it isn't ready.
strategies.use_when: an idea, a product or a pitch needs to land with real people.
steps: Ask the person to say the idea in one sentence a 12-year-old would get.
Cut every word that does not change the meaning.
Test it: "If someone hears only this, what will they do?"
Keep the long version for later. Lead with the short one.
strategies.inspired_by: Richard Branson, who says dyslexia helped him think big and keep his messages simple

strategies.name: Learn by changing roles
strategies.summary: See the problem from inside someone else's job.
strategies.use_when: the person wants to grow, or feels stuck in one way of seeing their work.
steps: Ask who else touches the problem: the customer, the seller, the builder, the boss.
Pick one role. Look at the problem from inside that role.
Ask: "What does this person see that you don't?"
For a career, suggest trying the role for real: a project, a workshop, a talk.

strategies.name: Learn by doing
strategies.summary: Try it first. Read about it only when you're stuck.
strategies.use_when: the person must learn a tool, a skill or a process, and the manual is a wall.
steps: Pick the smallest real task that uses the skill.
Do it together, one step at a time. Explain only what this step needs.
When something breaks, look it up then, and only that.
Do a second, slightly bigger task. Repeat.
strategies.inspired_by: Jamie Oliver, who is dyslexic and says "Get up and do something"

strategies.name: Learn from cases
strategies.summary: Remember a real example, not a rule.
strategies.use_when: a rule or a fact will not stay, but stories do.
steps: Skip the abstract rule. Start with one real case: who, what happened, what it cost.
Give a second case that is different in one way.
Ask the person what the two cases have in common. That is the rule.
Next time, ask them to recall the case, not the rule.
strategies.inspired_by: Narrative reasoning in The Dyslexic Advantage by Brock and Fernette Eide

strategies.name: Name it, don't number it
strategies.summary: Give things names you can picture, not codes.
strategies.use_when: people must remember many items, versions, projects or options.
steps: Find the codes and numbers people are struggling to remember.
Suggest a name for each one that carries a picture or a meaning.
Keep the names in one family, so they are easy to guess.
Use the names everywhere, and keep the codes only where a machine needs them.
strategies.inspired_by: IKEA founder Ingvar Kamprad, who was dyslexic and gave products names instead of numbers

strategies.name: Name what you need
strategies.summary: Say what helps you, plainly, before it's a problem.
strategies.use_when: the person needs something to do their best work, and has not said it.
steps: Ask what makes work easier for them: written follow-ups, more time, a call instead of a long email.
Turn it into one short, confident sentence. No apology.
Pick the right moment: a new job, a new manager, the start of a project.
Help them write the message, if they want.
strategies.inspired_by: David Flink, who has dyslexia and ADHD, founded the mentoring group Eye to Eye, and wrote Thinking Differently

strategies.name: Picture what you read
strategies.summary: Turn what you read into images, and remember the pictures.
strategies.use_when: the person must learn from a text, and the words slip away.
steps: Split the text into a few parts. One idea per part.
For each part, describe one clear image the person can hold: a place, an object, a scene.
Ask the person to change the image so it feels like theirs.
To review, ask them to walk through the images in order and say what each one means.

strategies.name: Read with your ears
strategies.summary: If reading is slow, listen instead.
strategies.use_when: there is a lot to read, and reading it is slow or tiring.
steps: Ask what needs to be read, and how long it is.
Suggest a way to listen: the phone's read-aloud, an audiobook, or a spoken summary from Claude.
For a long document, Claude first gives the answer and the to-dos, then the person listens to the parts that matter.
Afterwards, ask one question to check it went in.
strategies.inspired_by: the Yale Center for Dyslexia and Creativity, which lists text-to-speech and recorded books as accommodations, and Charles Schwab, who listens to audiobooks

strategies.name: Repeat until it sticks
strategies.summary: Go over it again, a different way each time.
strategies.use_when: something must be learned or remembered, and once is not enough.
steps: Say it plainly: going over it many times is a method, not a weakness.
Break the thing into small pieces.
Go over one piece several times, in a different way each time: read it, say it, draw it, use it.
Come back to it later. Ask the person to explain it back in their words.

strategies.name: Run the movie forward
strategies.summary: Play the future in your head, and watch where it breaks.
strategies.use_when: a decision depends on how things will change over time.
steps: Set the scene: "It's three months from now. You chose option A."
Play it forward in short scenes: next week, next month, next quarter.
Stop where something goes wrong. That is the risk to plan for.
Rewind, and play option B the same way.
strategies.inspired_by: Dynamic reasoning in The Dyslexic Advantage by Brock and Fernette Eide

strategies.name: Start from the end
strategies.summary: Picture it done, then walk backwards.
strategies.use_when: the goal is clear but the path to it is not.
steps: Ask the person to picture the finished result. "It's done. What do you see?"
Ask: "What had to happen just before that?"
Repeat, walking backwards, until you reach something they can do today.
Show the chain from today to the end.
strategies.shared_by: starter strategy, written for v0.1.0. Waiting for community stories.
strategies.inspired_by: the novelist John Irving, who is dyslexic and does not begin a novel until he knows the ending

strategies.name: Talk it out
strategies.summary: Say it before you write it.
strategies.use_when: the thoughts are there, but writing them down blocks them.
steps: Invite the person to talk or type freely, in any order. Voice dictation is great for this.
Do not interrupt or correct. Ask "and then?" or "why?" to keep it flowing.
When they stop, play it back as 3 to 5 clear points.
Ask: "Is that what you mean? What's missing?"
strategies.shared_by: starter strategy, written for v0.1.0. Waiting for community stories.

strategies.name: Tell it as a story
strategies.summary: Put the facts inside a story people remember.
strategies.use_when: people need to understand an idea, remember it, or care about it.
steps: Find the person in the story: who has the problem?
Say what they want, and what stops them.
Say what changes, and what their life looks like after.
Put facts and numbers inside the story, not before it.
strategies.shared_by: starter strategy, written for v0.1.0. Waiting for community stories.

strategies.name: Think in pictures
strategies.summary: Turn the problem into a drawing.
strategies.use_when: an idea is abstract, or words are going round in circles.
steps: Ask: "If this were a place or a machine, what would it look like?"
Turn the answer into a simple drawing or diagram.
Move things in the picture to test ideas. "What if this box were bigger?"
Bring the answer back into words at the end.
strategies.shared_by: starter strategy, written for v0.1.0. Waiting for community stories.
strategies.inspired_by: Charles Schwab, who says he is real good at concepts and visualization, and In the Mind's Eye by Thomas G. West

strategies.name: Train it another way
strategies.summary: Practise the weak skill through something you enjoy.
strategies.use_when: a skill is weak, and practising it directly is slow or painful.
steps: Name the skill underneath the task: memory, coordination, focus, order.
Find an activity that trains the same skill in a different way, often one the person enjoys.
Suggest it as practice, alongside the main task.
Connect it back: show where the trained skill helps in the real task.

strategies.name: Use the context
strategies.summary: When a piece is missing, read the whole picture around it.
strategies.use_when: a word, a fact or a detail is missing, but the situation around it is clear.
steps: Do not stop at the missing piece. Look at everything around it.
Ask: "Given all of this, what must the missing piece be?"
Make a best guess, and say how sure you are.
Check the guess against one more clue.
strategies.inspired_by: Carol Greider, Nobel Prize winner in 2009, who says dyslexia taught her to pull information out of context and put ideas together

strategies.name: What is this like?
strategies.summary: Borrow the answer from another area of life.
strategies.use_when: a problem feels new and there is no obvious method.
steps: Ask: "What else does this remind you of? It can be from any area of life."
Take the connection seriously. Ask how that other thing is solved.
Bring that solution back and test it on the real problem.
If the match breaks, say where, and try another connection.
strategies.shared_by: starter strategy, written for v0.1.0. Waiting for community stories.

rows.example: Write the product goal in one line, then place every request under it
A pre-mortem: it's launch day plus one month, and it went wrong. What happened?
Write the announcement customers will read, then work back to the spec
Map who wants what from whom, and find the knot
Watch three customers try it, before reading another dashboard

rows.moment: A gut feeling about the market
rows.example: Write the hypothesis, then the cheapest test that could prove it wrong

rows.moment: Pitching a feature to the team
rows.example: Explain the problem through a scene everyone knows
Replace "Epic 4.2" with a name people can picture
Keep three real customer stories, not forty quotes
Name your strongest guess, then the one log line that would prove it
Map the main modules and the calls between them before reading files
Trace a request through the system after your change, step by step
Spike both for an hour, and compare what you learned
Explain the problem out loud, line by line, before reading more

rows.moment: A ticket that makes no sense
rows.example: Reproduce it yourself, or ask the person who saw it
Read the callers and the tests around it before the code itself

rows.moment: A long design doc to review
rows.example: Listen to it once, then read only the parts that matter
Follow one user request from the click to the database and back

rows.moment: A long brief or research report
rows.example: Turn each finding into one image or sketch
Be the user for ten minutes, on a busy day
Walk through the flow as the user, screen by screen
Paper prototype first, before any pixels
Sketch three directions, at least one of them strange
Show the experience as a scene from a user's day
Pick three users whose stories show the pattern
Who is the user, what stops them, what changes now
Borrow a pattern from a product in another field
One sentence on where the company must be in a year
The whole idea in one sentence a 12-year-old would get
List what drains you, and who could own each part
Play each option six months ahead, and watch where it breaks

rows.moment: A big goal and no plan
rows.example: Picture the goal reached, then walk back to this month
Spend a morning where your product is used

rows.moment: Explaining a change to the team
rows.example: Who is affected, what changes for them, what stays the same

rows.example: One clear sentence, early, without apology
